blocks.text: Landsteiner discovered the ABO system in 1901. He found two antigens on red blood cells, antigen-A and antigen-B: some people had antigen-A, others antigen-B, and many had neither. Later his students found that some people have both. The groups were named A (antigen-A), B (antigen-B), AB (both) and O (neither).

Each person's plasma contains antibodies against the antigen he or she does not have: group A has anti-B antibodies and group B has anti-A antibodies. This is Landsteiner's rule of the antigen-antibody relationship.
Inheritance of the ABO blood groups

The ABO system is controlled by the gene I ('I' stands for iso-haem-agglutinogen), located on chromosome 9, with the multiple alleles IA, IB and i. IA and IB are co-dominant with each other and i is recessive to both. IA makes antigen-A, IB makes antigen-B and i makes no antigen.

blocks.alt: A table of the four ABO groups. Group A: genotype IA IA or IA i, square A antigens on the red cell, anti-B antibody. Group B: IB IB or IB i, triangular B antigens, anti-A. Group AB: IA IB, both antigens, no antibody. Group O: i i, no antigen, anti-A and anti-B. Below: DD or Dd is Rh-positive, dd Rh-negative; O-negative is the universal donor and AB-positive the universal recipient.
blocks.caption: ABO groups with their genotypes, antigens and antibodies, and the Rh groups (original diagram after Figures 18.4 and 18.5).
blocks.long_description: The I gene on chromosome 9 has three alleles: IA makes antigen A, IB makes antigen B, and i makes neither; IA and IB are co-dominant and both are dominant to i. Plasma carries antibodies against the ABO antigen a person lacks: group A has anti-B, group B anti-A, group AB neither and group O both. In the Rh system, allele D gives the Rh (D) antigen, so DD and Dd are Rh-positive and dd is Rh-negative; anti-Rh antibodies form only after an Rh-negative person meets Rh-positive cells. O-negative red cells carry no A, B or Rh antigen, so they can be given to anyone; AB-positive plasma has no anti-A, anti-B or anti-Rh, so it can receive any group.

blocks.text: Principle of transfusion in the ABO system

If unmatched blood is given, the recipient's antibodies attack the antigens on the donor's red cells and make them clump (agglutination). This happens if group A receives group B or the other way round, and if the donor is AB and the recipient is A, B or O.

items: Group O as donor has no antigen-A or antigen-B, so it can be given to A, B, AB or O: group O people are the universal donors of the ABO system.
Group AB as recipient has no anti-A or anti-B antibodies, so it can receive all types: group AB people are the universal recipients of the ABO system.

blocks.text: The book explains the high frequency of i through crosses that all produce group O children: ii x ii gives only group O; IA i x IA i, IB i x IB i and IA i x IB i each give 25% group O (ii).

blocks.title: For information
blocks.text: Some people secrete the A and B antigens into body fluids such as saliva, tears and urine; they carry a dominant secretor gene 'Se' on chromosome 19. The book also states that anti-A and anti-B antibodies form without exposure to the antigens, from embryonic life onward; most accounts place their appearance in the first months after birth.

blocks.prompt: A man of group A and his wife of group B have four children, each of a different blood group. How is this possible?
blocks.explanation: Both parents are heterozygous: IA i x IB i gives IA IB (AB), IA i (A), IB i (B) and i i (O), each with probability 1/4.

blocks.prompt: A woman of group B has a group O child. What are the genotypes of mother and child, and which genotypes could the father not have?
blocks.explanation: Child i i; mother IB i. The father must have given an i, so he cannot be IA IA, IB IB or IA IB.

items: IA and IB co-dominant, i recessive; gene I on chromosome 9.
Plasma has antibodies against absent ABO antigens.
O universal donor, AB universal recipient (ABO).
